# Orchestration — Delegate, Parallelize, Verify

_Applies when: doing any implementation work with Claude Code or OpenCode — this is the default operating posture, not only for big tasks._

The orchestrator (main instance) **delegates and verifies — it does not implement.** Workflows and
subagents are the **default**, not a fallback for large tasks: it reads, plans, asks the deciding
question, dispatches, verifies, integrates. There is an agent for every kind of work; it writes code
itself **only in a genuine emergency** (delegation truly unavailable), via the audited marker below.

## Default operating mode

- **Delegate by default** — agents write code, tests and migrations: **Workflow** for multi-step or
  parallel work, **subagents** for focused tasks. **Plan-first**: approval gate before architecture changes.
- **Parallelize** independent work over disjoint slices/domains, then synthesize; avoid shared-barrel /
  same-file collisions. Keep the main context lean — conclusions, not every sub-task transcript.
- **Adversarially verify** before trusting — a second pass (or a separate agent) checks the first;
  green tests alone are not proof. Ask the critical questions first, one decision per round.
- **A red signal is not proof either** — the mirror of `30-quality`'s bar against a **success**
  report: an IDE/language-server diagnostic on a file an agent is still writing is a mid-write
  snapshot with file:line and no currency (half-written syntax errors, "unused" symbols wired up
  three times). Re-run `tsc`/`lint` after its completion message; never pass one on as a finding.
- **Same lifecycle every session:** Definition of Ready before any dispatch (`21-session-lifecycle`),
  the fixed close sequence at the end (`22-session-close`), memory every time (`23-memory-discipline`).
- **Set the delegation model on every Workflow `agent()` call** — a fan-out step that omits it does
  **not** inherit the canonical delegation model (`06-model-effort`).

## Consolidate shared semantics — partitioning by slice is NOT sufficient

Whenever **2+ agents touch the same contract, protocol or algorithm**, "both fixed it" does not mean
consistent — and each still reports a green gate. Verified twice: two agents fixed one spec'd bug
**differently** → unbounded broadcast ping-pong that unit + E2E stayed blind to (structure converged,
just infinitely often), caught only by the orchestrator's manual diff; and one v2 slot shape in **4
copies** diverged **three** ways in one run — HTTP 400 on every v2 layout, v2 profiles skipped
**silently**, ZodError on save (in full: `skill:contract-golden-test`). Prefer, in this order:

1. **Serialize** — one agent authors the canonical artifact, N agents consume it.
2. **Generate** — derive the copies mechanically from that one source.
3. **Golden test** — the **floor, not an alternative**; 1–2 are the better fixes layered on top.
4. **Consolidation stage** — an agent diffs + aligns, the **last** resort. It can miss things too.

> Shim/mirror of a shared contract? A golden test against ONE shared fixture set is mandatory in EVERY
> consumer's gate — a renderer/unit test misses shim drift; only build→serialize→validate→read does.

**Review check:** grep the same type/schema definition across packages — every copy needs the SAME
golden-fixture import; one that forgets it stays invisible. **Diff the results, pick the canonical one, align the rest.**

## Content vs arrangement — inline is for orchestration, not implementation

- Producing the **content** of a change (code, tests, migrations) is **implementation → delegate**;
  deciding **which changes combine and whether they are correct** is **integration → orchestrator
  work**: merge/rebase/conflicts, release mechanics, reconciling subagent reports, cross-repo sync.
- **The honest grey zone:** *semantic* conflict resolution is authorship — hand it back to the agent
  that wrote that side. *Mechanical* resolution (imports, changelog lines) is orchestrator work.
- **Never write production code, tests or migrations inline when an agent could** — "it's only a small
  edit" is not an exception. **Hard-enforced on both targets:** Claude denies the main session's
  `Edit`/`Write` via a PreToolUse guard hook, OpenCode sets `agent.build.permission.edit = "deny"` on
  `build`; nothing is carved out, **`memory/` included** — even the close ritual's own entry is
  delegated. `bash` stays free for inspection and orchestrator work — never to smuggle edits past it.
- **The emergency exit is audited, not a loophole** (ADR-0023, Claude):
  `printf 'why' > "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/agent-core-emergency-inline"` — never the literal `.git/…`
  (a FILE in a worktree). Reason mandatory, TTL 60 min from mtime; empty or expired ⇒ still denied, and
  every allowed edit announces itself. No git dir? `AGENT_CORE_EMERGENCY_INLINE="why"`. **Delete the
  marker the moment delegation works again** — a forgotten one is how a guard rots into fail-open.
  OpenCode's deny is static config: an escape needs `opencode.json` + restart (`60-orchestration-opencode`).

## Concrete patterns (tier ↔ team size: see `20-workflow.md`)

- **Survey → synthesize:** N read-only agents over different areas, the orchestrator merges.
  **Find → verify:** one agent locates a bug/root cause, a second confirms it before any edit.
  **Plan → implement → review:** senior plans the spec, workers implement 1:1, QA checks the AC.
- **Parallel writers:** disjoint slices, one implementer each; the orchestrator integrates, runs the
  green gate once, **and consolidates every shared contract they all touched** (see above).
- **Bugfix:** debugger analyzes → worker fixes → senior reviews. **Lite:** one senior plans +
  implements, QA reviews. **Full:** PO spec → seniors plan ∥ → workers implement ∥ → QA → PO acceptance.
- **Council (wide solution space / high-stakes decisions):** convene the `llm-council` skill — N
  Claude-diverse members (Opus 5 · Opus 4.8 · Sonnet 5) answer independently, peer-rank each other's
  **anonymized** answers, a **chairman** (Opus 5) synthesizes. Standard per ADR-0031; complements
  `research-decide` as its deliberation engine. Not for trivial, fully-specified work.
- Cost-aware, not cost-blind: cheap inline *thinking* is fine, and pulling in only the agents a task
  needs caps the *number* of agents — never the **effort** or the model tiers of `06-model-effort`.
